core: LCA as a method to quantify environmental impacts across a product/service's whole life ('cradle to grave')
The life-cycle stages: raw material extraction, manufacturing, distribution, use, end-of-life
The four ISO 14040/14044 phases: goal and scope definition, life cycle inventory (LCI), life cycle impact assessment (LCIA), interpretation
Functional unit and system boundaries as the basis for fair comparison
How LCA reveals and prevents burden-shifting between stages or impact categories
Limitations: data quality/availability, assumptions, and boundary choices can change results; LCA does not decide cost or performance
supporting: The role of ISO 14040 (principles and framework) vs ISO 14044 (requirements and guidelines)
LCA supports but does not replace a broader decision process that weighs cost and performance
outOfScope: Detailed carbon-footprint accounting (owned by the Carbon Footprints topic; LCA is broader and multi-impact)
The circular-economy model itself (owned by the Circular Economy topic)
ESG and corporate sustainability reporting frameworks (owned by Corporate Sustainability/ESG)
Reproducing ISO standard text or specific impact-model equations

claims.claim: EPA defines LCA as a systematic, phased approach to quantify environmental impacts across the whole life of a product, process, or service, 'cradle-to-grave' — from raw-material extraction and energy production through use and final disposition.
EPA describes the LCA process as four components: goal definition and scoping, inventory analysis, impact assessment, and interpretation.
ISO 14040:2006 sets out the principles and framework for LCA and ISO 14044:2006 specifies the requirements and guidelines; both are 2006 international standards under environmental management.

LCA results are organized in terms of a functional unit that describes the function of the product or process; when comparing products, each system must deliver an equal amount of product or equivalent service so the comparison is fair.

Because LCA encompasses all stages from raw-material extraction to final disposal, it lets decision-makers compare all major environmental impacts and avoid burden-shifting, where reducing impact in one stage inadvertently increases it in another.

EPA states LCA can be resource- and time-intensive, that data availability greatly affects accuracy, and that LCA will not determine which product or process is most cost-effective or performs best, so it should be one component of a broader decision process.
Converting LCA impact results to a single score requires value judgments, so results depend on assumptions and modeling choices.
System-boundary variants include cradle-to-gate (extraction through the factory gate, omitting use and end-of-life) and cradle-to-cradle (end-of-life feeds recycling or reuse back into the system).

positions: EPA (2006) labels the first phase 'goal definition and scoping' and the second 'inventory analysis'.
ISO 14040/14044 wording is commonly rendered as 'goal and scope definition', 'life cycle inventory (LCI)', and 'life cycle impact assessment (LCIA)'.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: These are the same four phases; the lesson uses the ISO phase names as primary and notes the EPA wording, since both describe an identical framework EPA attributes to ISO.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft treated 'life-cycle assessment' as a generic 'foundational concept' with placeholder definitions (e.g., 'a foundational Environmental Sustainability concept covered in this lesson') and taught no actual LCA method, phases, functional unit, or limitations.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced boilerplate with the actual LCA method: cradle-to-grave scope, the four ISO phases, functional unit, system boundaries, burden-shifting, and limitations.
Removed the circular, non-informative vocabulary definitions and wrote non-circular, source-backed ones.
Grounded every substantive claim in EPA and ISO sources.
rightsIssues: ISO 14040/14044 standard text is copyrighted; described the standards' purpose and structure only, reproduced no standard text.
EPA document is a U.S. government work (public domain), but the lesson prose is original synthesis, not copied.

sourceRecords.title: Life Cycle Assessment: Principles and Practice (EPA/600/R-06/060)
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, National Risk Management Research Laboratory
sourceRecords.notes: Canonical EPA reference (record dirEntryId=155087). Full report read as the EPA NEPIS PDF, Dockey P1000L86 (https://nepis.epa.gov/Exe/ZyPDF.cgi?Dockey=P1000L86.PDF). Supports the cradle-to-grave definition, the four LCA components (goal definition and scoping, inventory analysis, impact assessment, interpretation), the functional unit and equal-service basis for comparison, burden/impact comparison across all stages, and the stated limitations (data availability, not a cost/performance verdict, single-score value judgments). U.S. government work, public domain; original synthesis only.

sourceRecords.title: ISO 14040:2006 Environmental management - Life cycle assessment - Principles and framework
sourceRecords.notes: 2006 international standard establishing the principles and framework for LCA, including the four phases (goal and scope definition, LCI, LCIA, interpretation). Described from the official catalogue listing and corroborating secondary summaries; standard text is copyrighted and was not reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: ISO 14044:2006 Environmental management - Life cycle assessment - Requirements and guidelines
sourceRecords.notes: 2006 companion standard giving the requirements and guidelines for conducting the LCA phases defined in 14040. Described from the official catalogue listing; no standard text reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Life-Cycle Assessment (LCA) Program (EPA Science Inventory)
sourceRecords.notes: EPA program record describing LCA as an environmental accounting and management approach covering cradle-to-grave activities from raw-material extraction through production, distribution, use, reuse, and final disposal, and noting EPA's role in ISO 14000 development and the TRACI impact model. Supports the life-cycle-stages framing.
